questions.q: Why can't other workloads reliably talk to a Pod by its own IP address?
options: Pods are never assigned an IP address at all
Pod IPs change every time a Pod is replaced, such as during a rolling update
Pod IPs are encrypted and cannot be read by other Pods
kube-proxy blocks all direct Pod-to-Pod traffic by default
questions.explain: A Pod gets a new IP from the cluster's Pod network each time it's created, and that IP is gone once the Pod is deleted — exactly what happens on every rolling update. A Service exists to give that changing set of Pods one stable address.

questions.q: How does a Service decide which Pods currently sit behind it?
options: By matching the Pod name to the Service name exactly
By checking which node the Pod happens to be scheduled on
By watching the ReplicaSet's resourceVersion field
By matching the Pods' labels against the Service's selector
questions.explain: A Service's spec.selector is a label query. Kubernetes keeps an Endpoints/EndpointSlice object current with the IPs of every Pod whose labels match, regardless of what the Pods are named.

questions.q: What is true of a Service with type: ClusterIP, which is also the default when no type is set?
options: It gets a virtual IP that is reachable only from inside the cluster
It opens a fixed port on every node in the cluster
It automatically provisions a cloud load balancer
It requires an Ingress controller to function at all
questions.explain: ClusterIP gives the Service a virtual IP routable only within the cluster's Pod network — the right default for internal APIs, caches, and databases that only other in-cluster workloads need to reach.

questions.q: What does a NodePort Service add on top of what ClusterIP already provides?
options: A requirement that every Pod run on the same node
TLS termination for external HTTPS traffic
The same fixed port, by default in the 30000-32767 range, opened on every node and forwarded to the Service
DNS resolution for Pods, which ClusterIP does not provide
questions.explain: NodePort does everything ClusterIP does, plus opening one consistent port on every node's IP (30000-32767 by default), forwarding whatever arrives there to the Service's matching Pods.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe LoadBalancer as a superset of NodePort rather than a separate mechanism?
options: Because LoadBalancer Services bypass kube-proxy entirely
Because a LoadBalancer Service has the cloud provider provision a real external load balancer that targets the NodePort opened on every node
Because LoadBalancer is only available for TCP, never HTTP
Because LoadBalancer Services cannot use selectors
questions.explain: A LoadBalancer Service gets everything NodePort provides, and then asks the cloud provider's controller to stand up a real external load balancer in front of that NodePort — which is also why EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until provisioning finishes.
